text.p: McDonald's Corp. said Wednesday it will decentralize its U.S. operations into five geographic areas to move decision-making and accountability closer to the restaurant level, and announced the retirement of a top executive.
McDonald's executives said the reorganization of its U.S. business, in the face of intense competition among fast-food players, had been in the works for several months.

But the move comes two months after the fast-food giant ended most of its Campaign 55 national price promotion. Some franchisees had been critical of the campaign, which offered featured hamburgers for 55 cents, saying it did not build sales and hurt profit margins.
"It pre-dates Campaign 55," Jack Greenberg, chairman of McDonald's USA unit, said of the U.S. restructuring plan.

Greenberg, who took charge of McDonald's U.S. business last October, is becoming chief executive officer of that unit, a title he assumes from Edward Rensi. Rensi, who had been president and chief executive officer of the McDonald's USA unit, is retiring because of "personal family commitments," McDonald's said.
Rensi, who began as a "grill man" in a Columbus, Ohio, McDonald's in 1966, agreed to stay on as a consultant to help complete development of a new production system.

McDonald's said it will eliminate eight zone officer positions based in Oak Brook, Ill., to which its 40 U.S. operating regions have reported. Those regions will now report to the appropriate division presidents, McDonald's said.

The company, which has more than 21,000 restaurants worldwide and over 12,000 in the United States, said the division presidents will have full responsibility and accountability for the performance of their divisions.

Bob Srygley, a McDonald's franchisee with four restaurants in Arkansas, said he believed the U.S. reorganization would be positive. "The company is finally taking steps as far as accountability is concerned," he added.
Ron Steger, a partner with KPMG Peat Marwick LLP, who specialises in restaurant consulting, applauded McDonald's decision to move U.S. management into the field.
"This is probably the first in a series of corrective actions to be taken to reverse what's been a fairly long-term decline in same-store sales," Steger said.

McDonald's had six consecutive quarters of declining U.S. same-store sales through the end of 1996. After a rise in U.S. same-store sales in the first quarter, analysts estimated second-quarter U.S. same-store sales declined.

McDonald's also named several executives in its U.S. operations, including Claire Babrowski, senior vice president of restaurant systems; Patrick Flynn, executive vice president of strategic planning; and Raymond Mines, senior vice president of franchisee relations.

McDonald's also said that Thomas Glasgow, executive vice president and chief operations officer, and Thomas Dentice, executive vice president, are "changing their roles in the company" and are expected to become U.S. owner/operators.
A franchise source said Dentice had overseen McDonald's ombudsman programme, which mediated disputes between franchisees and the company. McDonald's would not elaborate on Dentice's role.
McDonald's stock closed off 69 cents at $48.06 on the New York Stock Exchange.
